summary: This RFC discusses security issues when variable bit rate audio is used with secure RTP, and suggests guidelines to reduce them. Packet sizes can reveal information even when the content is encrypted.

eli5.summary: Even in a sealed envelope, its size can hint what is inside. This gives advice for keeping secret audio from leaking through size.

questions: packet length leaks in encrypted audio
does variable bit rate audio leak information in srtp
what is voice activity detection overhang
subtitle: Why packet sizes of variable bit rate speech can leak what is said over encrypted SRTP, and how to reduce the leak.

tldr.problem: SRTP encrypts the payload of RTP packets but adds no padding, so a variable bit rate codec produces packet sizes that follow the speech and leak a small amount of information about it.
tldr.mechanism: Use constant bit rate where the risk matters, add a random overhang period when using voice activity detection, and otherwise pad all packets to the same size with at least one octet of RTP padding.
tldr.outcome: Application designers get clear guidance on when VBR audio is acceptable with SRTP and when it SHOULD NOT be used.

facts.label: Minimum padding
facts.value: At least one octet on every packet

today: RFC 6562 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Packet Size Leak
sections.content:
The Secure RTP (SRTP) framework encrypts the payload of an RTP packet and can add an authentication tag, but leaves the RTP header in the clear. None of the predefined encryption transforms use padding, so RTP and SRTP payload sizes match exactly.

With a variable bit rate (VBR) codec, the compressed packet length depends on the speech signal. That variation leaks a small amount of information about the speech, which is potentially a security risk. The RFC cites work showing that known phrases in an encrypted call using the Speex codec in VBR mode can be recognized with high accuracy in certain circumstances, and that approximate transcripts can be derived for some codecs. How far these results generalize is described as an open question.
sections.eli5: Encryption hides the words but not how big each packet is. Big and small packets can give away clues about what was said.

sections.title: How Serious the Risk Is
sections.content:
The risk depends heavily on the application. In the worst case, recognizing a prerecorded message from a known set of possible messages can reach near-perfect accuracy. Highly structured dialogs, where an eavesdropper knows only a handful of sentences are possible, are also exposed.

Recognizing unconstrained conversational speech from rate information alone is unreliable and computationally expensive at present, but appears possible in some circumstances, and the attacks are only likely to improve over time. The leak should also be weighed against other visible information, such as the source and destination IP addresses.
sections.eli5: If the snooper already knows the few things you might say, the clues are very useful. For free-flowing chat they are much harder to use, but snoopers will get better.

sections.title: When to Use VBR Audio
sections.content:
The application designer decides the trade-off between security and bandwidth overhead. As a general rule, VBR codecs are considered safe for low-value encrypted unstructured calls.

Applications with prerecorded messages that could be of any value to an eavesdropper (beyond standard greetings) SHOULD NOT use codecs in VBR mode. Interactive voice response (IVR) applications are particularly vulnerable because an eavesdropper could recognize the prompts. Applications conveying highly sensitive unstructured information also SHOULD NOT use VBR mode.

Variable rate coding is safe when it adapts to the network and not to the speech, for example for congestion control, where packet sizes and spacing stay constant unless network conditions change.
sections.eli5: Casual chats are fine. For secret or scripted audio, keep every packet looking the same. Changing size only because the road is busy, not because of what you say, is safe.

sections.title: Voice Activity Detection and the Overhang
sections.content:
Many speech codecs use voice activity detection (VAD) to suppress frames or send lower-rate comfort noise when the speaker is silent. On an encrypted signal, watching the pattern of voice activity reveals some information. This leaks less than VBR coding because only two rates are possible.

To reduce the leak, an RTP sender using VAD with encrypted SRTP audio SHOULD add an unpredictable overhang period at the end of each talkspurt, delaying the start of silence or comfort noise by a random interval. The overhang audio must be packetized so that it is indistinguishable from the rest of the talkspurt. It SHOULD have an exponentially decreasing probability distribution, and a half life of a few hundred milliseconds is RECOMMENDED.

An overhang cannot be applied to the start of a talkspurt without hurting intelligibility, so some information about start times still leaks. For that reason VAD SHOULD NOT be used in encrypted IVR applications where prerecorded messages may be of value to an eavesdropper. The RFC still expects VAD to give significant bandwidth savings for many encrypted sessions.
sections.eli5: When you stop talking, keep sending sound for a random little while longer. Then a listener cannot tell exactly how long each word was.

sections.title: Padding the Output of VBR Codecs
sections.content:
Where VBR is considered unsafe, a constant bit rate (CBR) codec SHOULD be negotiated and used, or the VBR codec SHOULD be run in a CBR mode. If the codec has no CBR support, RTP padding SHOULD be used to bring the leak down to an insignificant level.

Packets may be padded to one constant size, to a small range of sizes, or to a size that varies with time. The most secure and RECOMMENDED option is to pad all packets throughout the call to the same size. One cited study achieved good results by padding to the next multiple of 16 octets, but the amount needed depends on the codec and the attacker. If padded sizes vary over time, padding SHOULD NOT be reduced without waiting a random hold time, and the RECOMMENDED hold time is the same as for VAD.

SRTP encrypts the count of padding octets, but not the bit in the RTP header that says a packet is padded. So it is RECOMMENDED to add at least one octet of padding to all packets in a stream, so an attacker cannot tell which packets needed padding.
sections.eli5: Stuff every envelope with filler until they are all the same size. Do it to every envelope, even the full ones, so nobody can tell which ones needed filler.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the entire memo is about security, and that the security considerations of RFC 3711, the SRTP specification, also apply. In the acknowledgements it notes that ZRTP (RFC 6189) has similar recommendations, and that this memo exists to bring them to a wider audience since they are not specific to ZRTP.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about staying safe. It also reminds you that the normal secure-audio rules still apply.

viz.caption: WAYS TO REDUCE THE PACKET SIZE LEAK

items.title: Use CBR
items.text: Negotiate a constant bit rate codec, or run the VBR codec in a CBR mode.

items.title: Pad to one size
items.text: The most secure and RECOMMENDED option is to pad all packets to the same size.

items.title: Random overhang
items.text: With VAD, delay the start of silence by a random interval at the end of each talkspurt.

items.title: Always pad
items.text: Add at least one octet of padding to every packet so padded ones are not visible.
